title: CLI Studios App Redesign
summary: Redesigned CLI Studios' dance-education app after tracing five usability problems to one root cause: over-reliance on modals that collapsed the information architecture. Rebuilt the IA first — four peer sections, full-page views replacing modals — before any visual pass, delivering a 13-page, 125+ component design system. A solo engagement.

angles.product: Five separate usability complaints turned out to be one architectural problem — an over-reliance on modals — so the fix was structural (eliminate modals, rebuild the IA) rather than five point-fixes, with the visual pass deliberately done last.

mine: Led a heuristic evaluation against Nielsen's 10 principles, then user interviews to validate the findings
Determined every usability problem was a symptom of one architectural flaw — over-reliance on modals
Decided to eliminate modals entirely, replacing them with full-page views and consistent back navigation, before touching visual clarity
Renamed content types to match user mental models, e.g. 'Courses' → 'Learning Path', 'Collections' → 'Playlists'
Explicitly rejected three alternative approaches — a visual refresh only, improving the modals, and five separate point-fixes — and documented the reasons for each
Built the 13-page design system documenting 125+ components, interaction patterns and accessibility specs

metrics.label: projected reduction in dev time from component reuse

metrics.label: root structural problems solved — IA rebuilt, modals eliminated, navigation simplified

narrative.problem: CLI Studios' dance-education app had collapsed under its own modals — users couldn't tell content types apart, navigate confidently, or recover from wrong turns. Root cause: an over-reliance on modal views had collapsed the information architecture.
built: 4 clear sections: Home, Discover, Library, My Pick

_notes: Solo engagement per the page ('no team to argue with'); contribution.team omitted rather than using the boilerplate.

The page explicitly states dev-time savings are unmeasured and adoption ('a system only becomes a system when someone uses it') had not yet been observed at time of writing; the 25% figure is recorded with confidence 'unverified' per the page's own framing.
